Now jump ahead a few days.
A city on a wide river, under a great suspension bridge.
Its windows still glow, powered by fuel burning in the dark.
Above it, the sky would be full of stars, day and night.
The temperature here would drop below zero, and keep going.
The river would be the first to change.
Ice would form along the banks, then reach out toward the middle.
Ice floats, so the river would freeze from the top down.
Beneath it, the water would stay liquid, as if under a lid.
Fish would gather in the deep water, where it stays a few degrees above freezing.
Minus ten.
Car engines would struggle to start.
Pipes would freeze and burst.
Buses and trains would slow down, then stop running.
Your breath would hang in the air like smoke.
The city would grow quieter every day.
Snow on the roads would never melt.
Not even by day, because there is no day.
The steel of the bridge would shrink in the cold, creaking as it settles.
By the end of the first week, the average temperature on Earth would be about minus seventeen degrees.
Colder than almost any winter most of us have ever known.
And not just here.
Everywhere on Earth, at the same time.
And it would only be the beginning.
